messages.content:
Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "1. Meeting at North Quay Bus Station

I met Mara at North Quay Bus Station on a rainy Tuesday morning, just before nine. We had agreed to inspect the passenger signs together because she was preparing a small access guide for the neighborhood library. The station serves local routes as well as coaches to nearby towns, and its entrance opens onto a broad paved forecourt. From there, three doors lead into the main concourse. I arrived by the eastern entrance, where a blue panel listed departures but did not show the location of the ticket office. Mara came in from the taxi rank carrying a folded station map and a notebook with a bright orange cover.

At the information desk, a staff member named Leon greeted us and asked what we were looking for. Mara explained that we wanted to follow the route a first-time visitor might take from the entrance to a platform. Leon pointed out a large overhead board, then showed us a smaller directory beside the desk. The board displayed destinations and departure times, while the directory identified the toilets, café, lifts, and ticket office. “People usually find the platforms once they know their route number,” he said. “The harder part is working out which side of the building they need.” He offered us a paper map, but Mara preferred to note the signs herself.

We began at the eastern doors and followed the arrows toward the central hall. The first sign used a bus symbol and the words “Local departures,” while a second arrow pointed toward “Coach bays.” Both were easy to see from the entrance, although a hanging advertisement covered part of the smaller directory when viewed from the left. We stopped near a row of benches to compare the printed map with the signs above us. The map marked the platforms with letters, but the overhead board used numbers for individual bays. Mara wrote down that difference and circled the point where the route appeared to change from letters to numbers.

The ticket office was beyond the central hall, opposite a café called Platform Kitchen. Its sign was mounted above a narrow doorway and could be missed by someone looking only at the larger departure board. A woman with a green suitcase asked us whether she could buy a ticket for the 10:15 coach to Wrenford there. Mara showed her the directory, and the woman checked the time on the board before walking to the office. She thanked Mara and said she had come in through the south entrance, where she had not seen any direction signs. We added the south entrance to our notes as a place to check on a later visit.

From the ticket office, we looked for the lifts. The nearest lift was behind a tiled column, with a small sign at eye level and another one fixed above the passage. Leon explained that the station had moved a vending machine recently, which had changed the clear walking line past the column. He said staff were collecting comments about the new arrangement. We tried the route with Mara pulling her wheeled case behind her. The case passed easily, but the lower sign was partly hidden when a tall man stood beside the column. The upper sign remained visible from the hall, so we recorded both observations rather than treating the lift as difficult to find in every circumstance.

We took the lift to the upper walkway, where the numbered bays were arranged along two sides. A digital screen displayed route numbers, destinations, and boarding times. The bay signs repeated the numbers in large white lettering on dark blue panels, and smaller labels named the operator for each route. At bay 12, a driver was checking a paper list beside a coach bound for Bellhaven. Mara asked whether passengers for Bellhaven should wait at the marked bay even when the coach was not yet present. The driver said, “Yes, the display updates when boarding is close, but the bay number stays the same.” We noted his explanation as useful context for readers who might arrive early.

On the return walk, we tested the route from the upper walkway back to the taxi rank. A yellow line on the floor led toward the stairs and lift, but it stopped at the main landing. Beyond that point, a sign directed passengers to the forecourt without distinguishing between the taxi area and the pickup lane. Near the south doors, a driver loading two suitcases told us that visitors sometimes waited in the wrong place because both areas were visible through the glass. Mara asked him where he usually sent them. He pointed toward a freestanding sign outside and said that its arrow faced the road, not the doors. We could see the sign from the pavement but not from inside the station.

Before leaving, we returned to Leon’s desk and compared our notes with the map. He listened as Mara described the covered directory, the letter-and-number change, and the signs by the lift. He said the station team reviewed wayfinding comments at regular staff meetings, but he did not know when the next sign update would take place. Mara copied down the station’s public feedback address from a card on the desk. We left through the south entrance, crossed the forecourt toward the taxi rank, and watched a family pause beside the glass doors to check the freestanding sign before choosing a direction.", "output": "1.
